name: Psychological pricing
statement: A price ending in 9 is supposed to sell more than the round price a cent higher, because shoppers read the left digit first and file $3.99 nearer to three dollars than four.
meaning: Two claims sit inside the practice, and Stiving and Winer separated them in 1997. A level effect says the 9 makes the price seem lower than it is, because consumers underestimate the value of the price. An image effect says the 9 carries meaning: consumers infer something from the right-hand digits, that the item is cheap, discounted or on offer, whatever the arithmetic. The two accounts predict different things. Under a level effect the ending works by fooling a calculation, so it should fade wherever the customer knows the price. Under an image effect it works by signalling, so it should fade wherever the signal is redundant or unbelievable, and it should be spent sparingly. Just-below prices are close to universal in retail. In a pilot scrape of their own, Troll and colleagues extracted 12,491 prices from a large online store in the United States and a large supermarket chain in Germany, and found 64.5% just-below, 24.0% precise and 11.5% round.

origin.who: Eric T. Anderson and Duncan I. Simester
origin.note: The practice is far older than the evidence for it. Anderson and Simester date the interest of economists back over 65 years to Ginzberg in 1936, whose mail-order test they describe as producing varied results, with demand rising for some items and falling for others. Their own paper is the first set of large randomised field experiments on the question, and it is what most later citation rests on. The name 'left-digit effect' comes from Thomas and Morwitz two years later.

evidence: Anderson and Simester ran three split-sample experiments with two mail-order women's clothing catalogues owned by one company. Customers were randomised by zip+4 postal code and mailed catalogues identical except for price endings. The counts below are customers mailed; each model is fitted to item-by-version demand rows, 219 in Study 1, 422 in Study 2 and 924 in Study 3. Study 1 sent three versions to 20,000 customers each and varied 27 items in $1 steps; the $9 coefficient was 0.341 with a standard error of 0.170, about 35% more demand, or 0.9 extra units per item. Study 2 sent two versions to 31,250 customers each across 211 items and got 0.143 with a standard error of 0.039, worth 1.3 units on a base of 8.7, about 15%. Study 3 sent three versions to 90,000 customers each across 308 items and got 0.071 with a standard error of 0.030 for items with no sale sign, worth 1.2 units on a base of 16.9, about 7%. Strulov-Shlain later estimated the bias from retail scanner data on about 3,500 products sold by 25 United States chains, and found consumers respond to a one-cent rise from a 99-ending price as if it were more than a twenty-cent rise, with an average bias parameter of 0.22, a median of 0.21 and an interquartile range of 0.04 to 0.40. Thomas and Morwitz report five experiments whose abstract states that nine-ending prices are perceived as smaller only where the leftmost digits of the two prices differ, as in $2.99 against $3.00.

replication.headline: The catalogue experiments found the effect. The meta-analysis of the laboratory and online literature puts it at g = 0.13, and at g = -0.01 once publication bias is corrected, and two preregistered high-powered experiments since found nothing.
replication.detail: Troll, Frankenbach, Friese and Loschelder ran a preregistered meta-analysis of 69 studies, 362 effect sizes and 40,541 participants. Just-below prices raised purchase decisions by g = 0.13, with a 95% interval of 0.01 to 0.25. They improved price image (g = 0.28), left prices more often underestimated (g = 0.67), and did nothing to perceived quality (g = 0.004, interval -0.17 to 0.18). Four things about that headline matter more than its sign. It does not include the field experiments above: the authors excluded Anderson and Simester, and Strulov-Shlain, because neither compares the relevant outcomes between just-below and round prices. Heterogeneity was extreme, at I2 = 92.84% for purchase decisions, and 219 of the 362 p-values were not significant. The design carries almost all of the result: within-subject studies, where the same person sees both prices, gave g = 0.34, interval 0.11 to 0.57, while between-subject studies gave g = 0.02, interval -0.09 to 0.13. Trim-and-fill correction for funnel asymmetry moved the purchase-decision estimate to g = -0.01, interval -0.10 to 0.09. Split by setting, laboratory and online studies gave g = 0.13, interval -0.001 to 0.25, and the seven field studies gave g = 0.04, interval -0.14 to 0.22, though that split is not itself a significant moderator, at p = 0.40. Two later experiments found nothing on demand. Fenneman and colleagues ran a preregistered online experiment on lottery tickets, 390 completions and 266 analysed after exclusions, 4,788 purchase decisions, and report no support for either a left-digit or a perceptual-fluency effect. Escher, Troll, Henjes and Loschelder ran two preregistered experiments on German students, 284 and 417 analysed, and found no effect of price ending on purchase intention, F(2, 281) = 0.16 and F(2, 411) = 0.10, while precise prices such as 28.83 euros beat both round and just-below prices on price image. Precise prices are a separate literature, and the precision-bias entry here, no. 311, holds it.

study.cite: Troll, E. S., Frankenbach, J., Friese, M., & Loschelder, D. D. (2024). A meta-analysis on the effects of just-below versus round prices. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 34(2), 299-325.

limits: The strongest experimental evidence is narrow. All three Anderson and Simester experiments used women's apparel sold by mail order in the United States, from two catalogue titles under one owner, at an average price near $50. Inside that setting the effect is already conditional. It was worth 22% on items new to the catalogue and 10% on items carried in previous seasons. On footwear the coefficient was negative and not statistically significant. It did not transfer to a neighbouring ending: the authors report that $9.50 endings, introduced by a catalogue manager hoping for an extra 50 cents, reduced demand if anything. A plain 'Sale' cue beat the price ending, at 0.215 against 0.071 in the same model, and adding a 9 ending to a new item that already carried a sale sign was worth 3.9% against 8.5% without one. Outside catalogues the picture changes. Ngobo, Legohérel and Guéguen modelled 188,623 store-week observations covering more than 11,000 items in 102 grocery categories, from French scanner panel data at two retailers. They conclude that nine-ending prices do not influence choice at the item level on their own, and that the effect ran negative in expensive categories, at -0.07. Bray and Harris ran a field experiment in twelve UK stores, six raising their usual 9-endings to round prices, and report in a later paper of their own that sales rose in most instances when the prices were rounded up. On price level the meta-analysis is unhelpful rather than reassuring: the single-moderator slope was -0.03 per $100 with an interval from -0.07 to 0.01, so expensive goods are neither shown to be immune nor shown to be affected.
misreadings: The percentage in circulation is one dress. Applied writing on charm pricing quotes a lift of about 24%, sourced to an unnamed analysis from 2011, and retells the catalogue work as a single item priced at $34, $39 and $44. That item is row one of Anderson and Simester's four-dress pilot, which sold 21 units at $39 against 17 at $44 and 16 at $34. The pilot as a whole sold 66 units at $9 endings against 46 at $5 lower and 45 at $5 higher, which the authors call roughly 40% and treat as a reason to run an experiment rather than as a result. Their published coefficients give 35%, 15% and 7% across three studies of one design, which is the range a reader should hold. The second misreading is mechanical. The popular story is that the brain truncates the price. Anderson and Simester tested it by splitting prices into tens and dollars, and found the weight on the left digit was -0.0631 and on the right -0.0651. That difference was too small to detect, which they read as evidence against dropping-off and for the signalling account. The left-digit boundary condition is weaker in the aggregate than in the paper that named it: purchase-decision effects were g = 0.16 where the first digit moves and g = -0.02 where it does not, but the moderator itself was not significant, at p = 0.17. Sokolova, Seenivasan and Thomas find the bias is stronger when both prices are visible at once than when one must be retrieved from memory, which is the same pattern as the meta-analysis finding almost all of the demand effect in within-subject designs. A 9 ending is a claim of a bargain made to someone comparing two numbers on one page, and it is not a reliable way to sell more of anything to someone who is not.

Read in full from the scan on Anderson's Kellogg faculty page, which is an image scan; every figure quoted here was read from the page images as well as from the OCR text.

Thomas, M., & Morwitz, V. (2005). Penny wise and pound foolish: The left-digit effect in price cognition. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(1), 54-64. Closed at Oxford Academic and JSTOR, and no copy was found through Unpaywall, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar on 17 August 2026. The publisher abstract was read twice, at Oxford Academic and at EconPapers. The $3.59 against $3.60 comparison is quoted here from Troll and colleagues, who cite it to page 63.

Stiving, M., & Winer, R. S. (1997). An empirical analysis of price endings with scanner data. Journal of Consumer Research, 24(1), 57-67. Source for the level effect and image effect distinction, taken from the publisher abstract; the full text is closed and no copy was located through Unpaywall on 17 August 2026.

Schindler, R. M., & Kibarian, T. M. (1996). Increased consumer sales response though use of 99-ending prices. Journal of Retailing, 72(2), 187-199. The publisher abstract reports that 99 endings led to increased purchasing. The full text is behind a ScienceDirect block and was not retrieved from Elsevier, the Rutgers research portal or a mirror on 17 August 2026, so the 8% sales difference usually quoted from it, described as not statistically significant, is taken here from Troll and colleagues.

The twelve-store design is quoted here from Troll and colleagues and the result from the authors' own later paper.
